silver-containing phosphonated monolayers are efficient in preventing bacterial adhesion in vitro and in inhibiting bacterial colonization in vivo, without affecting cell adhesion and proliferation, osteogenic differentiation, or the biocompatibility of titanium implants.

the antibacterial activity of silver-containing coatings with subnanomolar silver exposure can be evaluated in vitro and confirmed in vivo, and that these coatings are biocompatible in vitro and in subcutaneous implantations in vivo.

the MDPA/Ag(NO3) coatings exhibit significant antibacterial efficiency and excellent biocompatibilty both in vitro and after implantation in mice, without compromising the biocompatibility of Ti implants.

the development of new antibacterial surfaces with minimal silver content, which are able to prevent bacterial colonization of medical devices and to maintain their biocompatibility, thus minimizing the risk of infection and reducing the use of antibiotics.
the development of antibacterial coatings for medical devices that are based on the controlled release of silver.
the development of antibacterial surfaces that are biocompatible, non-toxic and non-leachable.

the MDPA/Ag nanocoatings are promising for the reduction of implant-related infections.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

silver-containing phosphonated nanocoatings with subnanomolar silver content exhibit significant antibacterial properties in vitro and in a mouse infection model, while allowing osteoblast attachment and differentiation, and are not cytotoxic to fibroblasts.

we have demonstrated the potential of a silver-containing phosphonated monolayer for preventing biofilm formation on medical devices, without compromising their biocorrosion resistance or biocompatibility.
the silver-containing phosphonated titanium surfaces are promising candidates for reducing the risk of infection associated with implanted devices, while maintaining their biocompatibility.
The main takeaway from our work is that

it is possible to obtain a coating with minimal silver loading and antibacterial activity, without compromising biocompatibility, which is a key point to consider for the development of new coatings for the prevention of infections.
the MDPA/Ag(+) coating strategy is a promising approach for preventing bacterial colonization of medical devices.

the antibacterial activity of silver-containing coatings can be maintained at low silver loadings, while keeping biocompatibility, and that the coatings can be sterilized with ethylene oxide without affecting these properties.
